lessons.title: Cumulative frequency, box plots and histograms
lessons.summary: Draw and interpret cumulative frequency graphs to find the median and quartiles, construct and compare box plots, and draw and interpret histograms with unequal class widths using frequency density.
objectives: I can complete a cumulative frequency table and draw a cumulative frequency graph.
I can read the median, quartiles and interquartile range from a cumulative frequency graph.
I can draw a box plot from a five-number summary and compare two box plots in context.
I can calculate frequency density and draw a histogram with unequal class widths.
I can read frequencies from a histogram and estimate the number of values in part of a class.

activities.title: Cumulative frequency
activities.content:
## Running totals

**Cumulative frequency** is a running total of frequencies. It answers "how many values are **less than** this?"

Times taken by 80 runners (minutes):

| Time $t$ | Frequency | Cumulative frequency |
|---|---|---|
| $20 \le t < 25$ | 6 | 6 |
| $25 \le t < 30$ | 18 | 24 |
| $30 \le t < 35$ | 30 | 54 |
| $35 \le t < 40$ | 20 | 74 |
| $40 \le t < 45$ | 6 | 80 |

Each cumulative frequency is the previous one plus the new frequency. The last value must equal the total, 80.

## Drawing the graph

Plot each cumulative frequency at the **upper end** of its class: (25, 6), (30, 24), (35, 54), (40, 74), (45, 80). You may also plot (20, 0) at the start. Join the points with a **smooth curve** (or straight lines). The result is an S-shaped curve that never goes down.

Plotting at the midpoint is the most common error: the cumulative frequency of 24 means 24 runners took **less than 30** minutes, so it belongs at 30.

## Reading the graph

With $n = 80$ values:

- **Median**: read across from $\frac{n}{2} = 40$ on the vertical axis to the curve, then down. About 32.7 minutes.
- **Lower quartile (LQ)**: from $\frac{n}{4} = 20$. About 28.9 minutes.
- **Upper quartile (UQ)**: from $\frac{3n}{4} = 60$. About 36.5 minutes.
- **Interquartile range (IQR)** = UQ − LQ ≈ 7.6 minutes. It measures the spread of the **middle half** of the data and is not affected by extreme values.

To find how many runners took **more than** 38 minutes, read up from 38 (about 66), then subtract from 80: about 14 runners.

question.text: A cumulative frequency graph represents 120 values. On the vertical axis, which value should you read across from to find the upper quartile?
question.hint: The upper quartile is three quarters of the way through the data.

question.text: For the class $30 \le t < 35$ with cumulative frequency 54, where should the point be plotted on a cumulative frequency graph?
question.hint: Cumulative frequency counts values below the top of the class.
question.explanation: 54 values are less than 35, so plot (35, 54) at the upper class boundary.

options.feedback: Midpoints are for frequency polygons and estimated means, not cumulative frequency.
30 is the class frequency, not the cumulative frequency.

activities.title: Worked example: box plots
activities.content:
## The five-number summary

A **box plot** (box-and-whisker diagram) displays five values on a number line:

1. **Minimum**
2. **Lower quartile (LQ)**
3. **Median**
4. **Upper quartile (UQ)**
5. **Maximum**

The **box** runs from LQ to UQ with a line inside at the median; the **whiskers** extend from the box to the minimum and maximum.

For the runners: minimum 20, LQ 28.9, median 32.7, UQ 36.5, maximum 45. Draw a scale from 20 to 45, mark the five values, draw the box from 28.9 to 36.5 with a line at 32.7, and whiskers out to 20 and 45.

The box holds the **middle 50%** of the data; each whisker holds 25%. The **range** is max − min = 25; the **IQR** is the width of the box, 7.6.

## From a list of data

For a small data set, order the values and find the median, then the medians of the lower and upper halves.

$3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 14, 15, 20$: median 9 (5th of 9), LQ 5.5 (middle of 3, 5, 6, 8), UQ 14.5 (middle of 12, 14, 15, 20).

## Comparing two box plots

Make **two** comparisons, one about **average** (medians) and one about **spread** (IQR or range), and put both **in context**.

*Girls: median 32, IQR 6. Boys: median 35, IQR 11.*

"The girls' median time is lower, so on average the girls ran faster. The girls' IQR is smaller, so their times were more consistent."

Prefer the **IQR** to the range for spread, because the IQR ignores extreme values (outliers) and so describes the typical spread more fairly. Say this if asked why the IQR is a better measure.

question.text: A box plot has minimum 12, lower quartile 18, median 23, upper quartile 31 and maximum 40. Work out the interquartile range.
Find the upper quartile of the data set 4, 7, 9, 10, 13, 15, 18, 21, 22, 26, 30.
question.hint: 11 values: the median is the 6th (15). The upper half is the 5 values above it; take their middle.

activities.title: Histograms and frequency density
activities.content:
## Bars whose area shows frequency

A **histogram** displays grouped continuous data. It looks like a bar chart with **no gaps**, but there is a crucial difference: when the classes have **unequal widths**, the **area** of each bar represents the frequency, not the height.

The height is the **frequency density**:

$\text{frequency density} = \dfrac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$

and so $\text{frequency} = \text{frequency density} \times \text{class width}$.

## Drawing one

Masses of 60 parcels (kg):

| Mass $m$ | Frequency | Class width | Frequency density |
|---|---|---|---|
| $0 \le m < 2$ | 10 | 2 | 5 |
| $2 \le m < 3$ | 12 | 1 | 12 |
| $3 \le m < 5$ | 20 | 2 | 10 |
| $5 \le m < 10$ | 18 | 5 | 3.6 |

Draw the horizontal axis with a continuous scale (0 to 10), the vertical axis labelled **frequency density**, and bars of the given heights spanning each class, touching each other.

Notice that the $5 \le m < 10$ class has the second-highest frequency but the **lowest** bar, because it is spread over a wide interval. Reading heights as frequencies is the classic histogram mistake.

## Why frequency density?

Using plain frequency for bar heights makes wide classes look far more important than they are. Frequency density corrects for the width so the picture is fair: it shows how **crowded** each part of the scale is.

## The modal class

On a histogram, the modal class is the one with the **tallest** bar (highest frequency density), which here is $2 \le m < 3$ even though $3 \le m < 5$ contains more parcels.

question.text: A class $10 \le x < 25$ has frequency 36. Work out its frequency density.
question.hint: Frequency ÷ class width; the width is 15.

question.text: On a histogram, the bar for the class $40 \le x < 60$ has a frequency density of 1.8. How many values are in this class?

activities.title: Worked example: reading a histogram
activities.content:
## Finding frequencies and totals

A histogram of the ages of visitors to a museum has these bars: $0$ to $10$ with frequency density 2; $10$ to $20$ with density 5; $20$ to $40$ with density 3.5; $40$ to $70$ with density 1.5.

**How many visitors were there in total?**

Each frequency is density × width:

- $0$–$10$: $2 \times 10 = 20$
- $10$–$20$: $5 \times 10 = 50$
- $20$–$40$: $3.5 \times 20 = 70$
- $40$–$70$: $1.5 \times 30 = 45$

Total $= 185$ visitors.

## Part of a class

**Estimate how many visitors were aged between 30 and 40.**

This is half of the $20$–$40$ class. Assuming the ages are spread evenly within the class, take the area of the part of the bar from 30 to 40: $3.5 \times 10 = 35$ visitors.

**Estimate how many were over 55.** From 55 to 70 is 15 years of the last bar: $1.5 \times 15 = 22.5$, so about 23 visitors. It is an estimate because we do not know exactly how the ages are distributed inside the class.

## When the scale is missing

Sometimes the vertical axis has no numbers but you are told one frequency. If the $10$–$20$ bar (height 5 squares) represents 50 people, then each square of height on a width-10 bar is 10 people, and you can scale every other bar the same way. Work out what **one unit of area** is worth, then multiply.

## Histograms and the median

The median is the value that splits the total area in half. With 185 visitors, find where the cumulative area reaches 92.5: after the first two bars the total is 70, so 22.5 more are needed from the third bar at density 3.5: $22.5 \div 3.5 = 6.4$, so the median age is about 26.

question.text: A histogram bar covers the class $50 \le x < 80$ with frequency density 2.6. Estimate how many values lie between 65 and 80.
question.hint: Width of the part is 15; multiply by the density.

activities.title: Common mistakes
activities.content:
## Watch out for

- **Cumulative frequency plotted at midpoints.** Plot at the **upper** class boundary.
- **Reading the median from the wrong place.** Read across from $\frac{n}{2}$ on the **vertical** axis, then down to the horizontal axis.
- **Quartiles from $\frac{n}{4}$ and $\frac{3n}{4}$** of the total, not of the highest class.
- **Box plot whiskers to the quartiles** instead of the min and max.
- **Comparisons without context** or with only one comparison. Give a median statement and a spread statement, both about the real situation.
- **Histogram heights read as frequencies.** Height is frequency density; frequency is **area**.
- **Forgetting to label** the vertical axis "frequency density".
- **Class width errors.** The width of $5 \le m < 10$ is 5, not 10.
- **Estimates within a class.** State that the answer is an estimate assuming an even spread.

question.text:
The table shows the times, in minutes, that 200 customers spent in a shop.

| Time $t$ | Frequency |
|---|---|
| $0 \le t < 10$ | 30 |
| $10 \le t < 15$ | 50 |
| $15 \le t < 20$ | 60 |
| $20 \le t < 30$ | 40 |
| $30 \le t < 50$ | 20 |

(a) Complete the cumulative frequencies for the five classes.

(b) State the coordinates of the point you would plot for the class $15 \le t < 20$.

(c) Work out the frequency density for the class $30 \le t < 50$.

(d) A box plot for a rival shop shows a median of 21 minutes and an interquartile range of 14 minutes. From your cumulative frequency graph the median for this shop is about 16 minutes and the IQR about 11 minutes. Compare the times spent in the two shops.
question.hint: (a) Running totals. (b) Upper boundary, cumulative frequency. (c) Frequency ÷ width. (d) Two comparisons in context.
question.explanation: (a) 30, 80, 140, 180, 200. (b) (20, 140). (c) $20 \div 20 = 1$. (d) Customers in this shop spend less time on average (median 16 < 21), and their times are more consistent (IQR 11 < 14).

markScheme.criterion: Point (20, 140) plotted at the upper boundary
Compares medians in context: this shop's customers spend less time on average
Compares IQRs in context: this shop's times are more consistent / less spread

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Cumulative frequency** = running total; plot at the **upper** class boundary; join with a smooth curve.
- Median from $\frac{n}{2}$, LQ from $\frac{n}{4}$, UQ from $\frac{3n}{4}$ on the vertical axis; **IQR = UQ − LQ**.
- **Box plot**: min, LQ, median, UQ, max; the box holds the middle 50%.
- Compare distributions with a median statement and an IQR statement, both in context; the IQR is better than the range because it ignores extremes.
- **Histogram**: frequency density $= \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$; **area** = frequency; no gaps; label the axis "frequency density".
- Estimate part of a class by density × the width of that part.

practiceQuestions.text: Frequencies for four classes are 7, 15, 22 and 6. Write down the cumulative frequency for the third class.
A cumulative frequency graph shows 60 values. From which value on the vertical axis should you read across to find the median?
From a cumulative frequency graph, the lower quartile is 14.5 and the upper quartile is 27. Work out the interquartile range.
Put these five values in the order they appear from left to right on a box plot.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, maximum.

practiceQuestions.hint: The median is the 6th value (11). The lower quartile is the middle of the 5 values below it.

practiceQuestions.text: What fraction of the data lies inside the box of a box plot?
practiceQuestions.hint: The box runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Between the quartiles lies the middle 50% of the data.

practiceQuestions.text: A class $20 \le x < 24$ has frequency 30. Work out the frequency density.
A histogram has three bars: $0$ to $5$ with frequency density 4, $5$ to $15$ with density 3, and $15$ to $40$ with density 0.8. Work out the total frequency.
practiceQuestions.hint: Multiply each density by its class width and add.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: on a histogram with unequal class widths, the tallest bar always represents the class with the most values.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Height is frequency density; the frequency is the area. A wide, short bar can contain more values than a tall, narrow one.

practiceQuestions.text: Two classes of students sat the same test. Class A: median 58, range 70, IQR 15. Class B: median 58, range 40, IQR 24. Priya says Class A's results are more spread out because the range is larger. Explain why the IQR suggests otherwise and which measure is more reliable.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Class A's IQR (15) is smaller than Class B's (24), so the middle half of Class A's marks is less spread out; its large range is probably caused by one or two extreme marks. The IQR is more reliable because it is not affected by outliers.

markScheme.criterion: States that Class A has the smaller IQR so its middle 50% is less spread / more consistent
Explains the IQR is more reliable because it ignores extreme values / outliers, which inflate the range

practiceQuestions.text:
A histogram shows the distances (km) travelled by 150 people to a concert. The bars are: $0$ to $5$ with frequency density 8; $5$ to $10$ with density 6; $10$ to $20$ with density 3; $20$ to $50$ with density $d$.

(a) Work out the frequencies of the first three classes.

(b) Work out the value of $d$.

(c) Estimate the number of people who travelled more than 35 km.
practiceQuestions.hint: (a) Density × width. (b) The last class must contain the remaining people. (c) 35 to 50 is half of the last class.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) $40, 30, 30$. (b) Remaining $= 150 - 100 = 50$ people in a class of width 30, so $d = 50 \div 30 = 1.67$ (or $\frac{5}{3}$). (c) $\frac{5}{3} \times 15 = 25$ people.

markScheme.criterion: Estimate 25 people travelled more than 35 km
